If even one term—such as lock contention on an unmediated mutex ($B_i \to \infty$) or unscheduled direct memory access traffic competing for memory buses ($I_i \to \infty$)—lacks an analyzed mathematical upper bound, the system has no bound on its worst-case response time, however small the mean latency appears in statistical benchmarks.[^fn-math-liu-layland] When $R_i$ exceeds $D_i$, the real-time enforcer misses its execution slot. In the physical machine, a missed deadline freezes the motor inverters on stale setpoints, introducing phase erosion ($\Delta\phi = -\omega T_s / 2$) that destabilizes high-gain feedback loops. In the safety budget, if the enforcer is delayed by priority inversion or bus starvation, it cannot evaluate chunk freshness or command emergency deceleration on time: every millisecond that scheduling latency expands response delay directly consumes $v \cdot \Delta t$ ($1.5\text{ mm}$ per millisecond at the drive limit) of physical stopping clearance.

[^fn-math-liu-layland]: **Rate-Monotonic Scheduling**\index{Rate-monotonic scheduling}: @liu1973scheduling established that static-priority rate-monotonic scheduling guarantees periodic task schedulability when total processor utilization satisfies $U \le n(2^{1/n} - 1)$, converging to $\ln(2) \approx 0.693$ for large $n$. In distributed robotic architectures with arbitrary execution deadlines and shared resource blocking, systems engineers deploy exact Response Time Analysis ($R_i = C_i + B_i + I_i \le D_i$) to verify deterministic schedulability. For the formal mathematical derivation of response time recurrences, see @sec-appendix-systems.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Deterministic fieldbus jitter bounds provide the execution baseline for heterogeneous placement in @sec-placement-resource-contention.
:::

Bounding these terms requires categorizing every source of execution variance by whether its worst-case bound exists:

1. **Bounded Sources:** Admit analytical upper bounds from hardware specifications. Examples include fixed-pipeline instructions, round-robin bus arbitration, zero-wait-state tightly coupled memory (TCM/SRAM), and vectored interrupt dispatch on a bare-metal microcontroller.
2. **Experimentally Characterized Sources:** Cannot be proven from first principles but can be enveloped under locked hardware configurations. Examples include last-level cache misses under hardware cache line locking, write-buffer drains, periodic DRAM refresh cycles, and thermal throttling under closed-loop active cooling.
3. **Unbounded Sources:** Have no finite mathematical worst-case bound and must be purged from the real-time safety path. Examples include operating system page faults under demand paging, preemptive thread scheduling without priority inheritance (war story \ref{ws-nervous-1997-mars-pathfinder-priority-inversion}), general-purpose heap allocation over fragmented free lists, and unscheduled PCIe DMA crossbar contention.

In general-purpose Linux environments, the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) introduces unbounded execution jitter because it prioritizes threads based on virtual runtime (`vruntime`) rather than physical deadlines. Unshielded user-space threads running in managed runtimes (Python, Java/JVM) compound this: stop-the-world garbage collection passes and Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) contention cause thread freezes lasting from tens of milliseconds to seconds. Achieving a provably bounded worst-case execution time ($C_i$) requires eliminating runtime memory allocations, locking all process memory via `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE)`, shielding CPU cores via `pthread_setaffinity_np`, and assigning static real-time priorities under `SCHED_FIFO` or `SCHED_DEADLINE`.

::: {#ws-nervous-1997-mars-pathfinder-priority-inversion .callout-war-story title="The Mars Pathfinder priority inversion (1997)"}
**Context**: In July 1997, shortly after landing on Mars, the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft's avionics computer ran the VxWorks real-time operating system with preemptive priority-based scheduling across mission tasks [@reeves1997pathfinder].

**Mechanism**: A high-priority thread (`bc_dist`) distributed critical spacecraft bus telemetry, while a low-priority thread (`ASI/MET`) gathered meteorological sensor data through a shared mutex-protected pipe. When `ASI/MET` held the mutex, medium-priority tasks preempted it. Because they outranked the meteorological thread, they kept it from running while `bc_dist` blocked waiting for the mutex it held, an unbounded priority inversion.

**Impact**: The high-priority bus distribution task missed its deadline. When the `bc_sched` task started the next bus cycle and found `bc_dist` unfinished, the flight software reset the computer. Data already collected survived each reset, but the resets recurred until the software was changed.

**Response**: Engineers reproduced the reset on a ground replica of the spacecraft with VxWorks event tracing, then uploaded a patch that enabled priority inheritance [@sha1990priority] on the mutex semaphore.

**Systems lesson**: The medium-priority tasks kept the low-priority mutex holder from running, so the high-priority bus task could not progress. Priority inheritance let the holder finish and release the mutex. In a motor-control path, engineers must bound such blocking time ($B$) or remove the shared lock from the cycle-critical exchange.
:::

The same classification governs dynamic memory management. A general-purpose heap allocator (`malloc`/`free`) that traverses fragmented free lists exhibits search times dependent on execution history, rendering its worst-case latency unbounded. In contrast, a fixed-size block pool or a Two-Level Segregated Fit (TLSF) allocator provides deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1)$ allocation and deallocation bounds. The gold standard for the real-time permission path is a **zero-allocation static architecture**\index{Zero-allocation static architecture}, in which all buffers, ring queues, and state variables are allocated in static SRAM at compile time, eliminating runtime memory management entirely.

### Event-triggered and time-triggered bus architectures {#sec-nervous-fieldbus-architectures}

The communication fabric carrying commands from the enforcer to distributed motor drives contributes directly to the blocking term $B$ and interference term $I$ in Response Time Analysis. In physical AI, command transport is organized across a four-layer real-time communications hierarchy:

1. **Accelerator Host Interconnect (PCIe DMA):** High-throughput PCIe Gen4/Gen5 bus links exchange multi-gigabyte foundation model weights and sensory tensors between host CPU memory and neural accelerators. Scatter-gather DMA descriptors and MSI-X interrupt routing move gigabytes per second with bounded host CPU overhead.
2. **Inter-Process Shared Memory (POSIX SHM):** Unprivileged host proposers and real-time execution threads exchange trajectory chunks via POSIX shared memory (`shm_open`, `mmap`) and zero-copy shared memory fabrics (such as Eclipse Iceoryx). Lock-free single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffers and three-slot mailboxes eliminate kernel-space network socket buffering and dynamic heap allocations.
3. **Deterministic Actuator Fieldbuses (EtherCAT, TSN Ethernet):** Microsecond-level real-time fieldbuses transport cyclic joint commands and encoder telemetry across distributed servo drives within a guaranteed $1.0\text{ ms}$ bus cycle ($T_{\text{bus}}$) with sub-microsecond synchronization jitter ($\sigma_{\text{jitter}} < 100\text{ ns}$).
4. **Diagnostic and Auxiliary Telemetry Buses (CAN-FD):** Asynchronous priority-arbitrated buses manage lower-rate chassis subsystems (battery management systems, environmental monitors, auxiliary lighting) where non-preemptive arbitration delay is acceptable under bounded bus utilization.

Following Hermann Kopetz's taxonomy [@kopetz2011real], distributed fieldbus protocols divide into event-triggered and time-triggered paradigms:

* **Event-Triggered Architectures (e.g., CAN, CAN-FD):** Nodes transmit asynchronously whenever local state changes. Bus access is resolved via physical-layer bitwise arbitration (CSMA/CR). While high-priority messages preempt lower-priority arbitration, transmission is non-preemptive: an in-flight frame cannot be interrupted, forcing an emergency braking command to wait behind lower-priority telemetry. Furthermore, a malfunctioning node can flood the shared wire with continuous traffic (the "babbling idiot" failure), degrading bus determinism into millisecond-scale queuing jitter ($200\text{--}500\,\mu\text{s}$).
* **Time-Triggered Architectures (e.g., EtherCAT, Time-Sensitive Networking):** Communication follows a static Time-Division Multiple Access (TDMA) schedule synchronized to a global reference timebase. Each node transmits exclusively within its assigned temporal window, eliminating contention, queuing bloat, and transmission collisions ($I_{\text{bus}} = 0$).

A foundational architectural requirement in physical AI is contrasting **deterministic bus fabrics** (PCIe DMA, EtherCAT, CAN-FD) with **non-deterministic network transports** (standard switched Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and 5G cellular):

- **Non-Deterministic Network Transports (Switched Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 5G):** Standard local-area networks are optimized for statistical multiplexing and average throughput rather than bounded latency. In standard switched Ethernet (IEEE 802.3), packets compete for shared switch buffer queues. Under bursty traffic (such as uncompressed multi-camera vision frames), switch buffers experience buffer bloat, packet drops, and queuing jitter ranging from hundreds of microseconds to tens of milliseconds. Transport protocols like TCP enforce reliable delivery via acknowledgment tracking, introducing head-of-line blocking and exponential backoff retransmission storms under transient packet loss. Wireless links (Wi-Fi 6, 5G NR) compound this with physical-layer RF interference, beamforming adaptation pauses, and multipath fading. For a $1\text{ kHz}$ kinematic enforcer or a $20\text{ kHz}$ motor inverter, a single fifty-millisecond network hiccup is indistinguishable from a severed physical wire: motor inverters starve, phase lag collapses stability margins, and moving mass travels blind. Consequently, non-deterministic transports are strictly confined to high-level teleoperation proposals or cloud telemetry, and must never sit on the direct closed-loop actuation path.
- **Deterministic Bus Fabrics (PCIe DMA, CAN-FD, EtherCAT, TSN):** Direct-attached bus fabrics provide hardware-enforced latency bounds. Within the host compute node, co-located accelerators exchange multi-gigabyte model weights and sensory tensors across PCIe interconnects using scatter-gather DMA, moving data with bounded host interrupt overhead. Across distributed physical actuators, CAN-FD provides hardware bit-level priority arbitration for auxiliary chassis telemetry. For cycle-critical motor control, EtherCAT and Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) enforce microsecond-level time-triggered determinism, completely bypassing software protocol stacks and operating system schedulers.

::: {#fig-industrial-ethercat-controller fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Real-time distributed controller with modular I/O**: Dedicated embedded real-time controller and adjacent hardware I/O modules. The unit acts as a deterministic bus coordinator, synchronizing distributed sensor acquisition and motor drive terminals via hardware-scheduled Ethernet telegrams. (Photo: Oleg Yunakov, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Beckhoff_IoT_controller_CX5120.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0)." fig-alt="Photograph of an embedded real-time controller with Ethernet ports and modular I/O terminals."}
![](images/jpg/fig04_real_industrial_ethercat_controller.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

As illustrated in @fig-industrial-ethercat-controller, distributed real-time platforms physically decouple high-level host computing from localized sensor acquisition and motor drive peripherals. A central real-time processor acts as the communication bus coordinator, coordinating distributed peripheral nodes over a high-speed deterministic bus. Each peripheral node incorporates dedicated controller silicon that inspects and mutates passing network telegrams on the fly in hardware. Dedicated Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) circuits align distributed clocks,[^fn-hw-ethercat-dc] so that hardware synchronization pulses (`SYNC0`) fire local analog-to-digital conversions and PWM gate-drive updates across all distributed physical nodes to within sub-microsecond precision ($\le 50\text{ ns}$ jitter).

[^fn-hw-ethercat-dc]: **Distributed Clock**\index{Distributed clock}\index{Time-to-digital converter!timestamp synchrony}: Under IEC 61158-4-12, EtherCAT Distributed Clocks (DC) synchronize distributed servo drive nodes to a reference clock timebase by measuring physical propagation delays across the ring topology. Dedicated Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) units in each peripheral node controller latch arrival timestamps at physical transceiver pins when the Start of Frame Delimiter (SFD) traverses the port, allowing the bus coordinator to evaluate bidirectional delays ($t_{\text{prop}}$) and discipline local timers so that hardware `SYNC0` pulses fire simultaneously across all joint inverters within $\le 50\text{ ns}$. Clock alignment alone does not bound the complete control cycle, which must also account for controller response time and PWM gate update latency.

A frequent architectural mistake in physical AI is attempting to close inner motor control loops over general-purpose robotics middleware (such as ROS 2 over DDS or Zenoh). Publish-subscribe middleware provides powerful abstractions for dynamic node discovery, multi-modal introspection, and high-level sensory message passing. However, standard DDS implementations rely on dynamic heap allocation, variable serialization overhead, multi-tenant operating system network stacks, and asynchronous executor thread scheduling. Even with real-time thread priority and tuned Quality of Service (QoS) profiles, DDS introduces tens to hundreds of microseconds of software jitter—and potential millisecond-scale tail latency during network buffer bloat or retransmission storms. While middleware augmented with zero-copy shared memory transports (such as Iceoryx) or bare-metal implementations (such as micro-ROS) can link co-located processes or microcontrollers, closing high-gain current loops and multi-axis joint control requires dedicated, cycle-deterministic bus hardware rather than general-purpose network stacks.

### Protocol schedulability comparison between CAN-FD and EtherCAT {#sec-nervous-schedulability-analysis}

On the mobile manipulator the candidate communication links sort strictly by hierarchy:

1. **Board-Level Peripheral Interconnects (SPI, Memory-Mapped I/O):** Connects microcontrollers directly to joint encoders, current-shunt ADCs, and gate drivers with sub-microsecond latency ($< 1\,\mu\text{s}$) under a fixed transfer schedule.
2. **Deterministic Drive Command Buses (EtherCAT, TSN Ethernet):** Transports cyclic joint setpoints and sensor feedback across all distributed drive inverters within a guaranteed $1.0\text{ ms}$ bus cycle ($T_{\text{bus}}$) with sub-microsecond synchronization jitter ($\sigma_{\text{jitter}} < 100\text{ ns}$).
3. **Chassis and Auxiliary Diagnostic Buses (CAN-FD):** Manages lower-rate battery management systems (BMS), environmental sensors, and diagnostic telemetry where priority arbitration is acceptable under verified worst-case bus load.

None of these bounds belongs to a protocol acronym alone. Each depends on the configured devices, wiring, payload sizes, and schedule. The critical architectural question is whether all servo axes fit within the permission path's bus cycle budget.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-fieldbus-schedulability
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FIELDBUS SERIALIZATION OCCUPANCY: CAN-FD VS. ETHERCAT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-nervous-fieldbus-serialization-latency-wcet-schedulability
# │ Goal:    Quantify bus occupancy for the running machine's servo axes;
# │          full response time needs more terms.
# │ Show:    CAN-FD serialization = 1.264 ms vs. EtherCAT frame/hops = 33.6 us
# │          for 9 axes (7 arm joints + 2 drive wheels) in a 1 ms bus cycle.
# │ How:     Serialization and hardware forwarding models; axis count and
# │          bus cycle from RM, frame parameters are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_percent, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class FieldbusSchedulability:
    """Scenario serialization and forwarding occupancy, not end-to-end schedulability."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    num_axes = RM.servo_axes  # category: chosen (arm joints + drive wheels)
    arm_axes = RM.arm.dofs  # category: datasheet
    cycle_time = RM.fieldbus_cycle  # category: illustrative (EtherCAT cycle, T_bus)

    # Frame parameters below are scenario assumptions (chosen for this comparison)

    # CAN-FD parameters
    canfd_payload_64 = 64  # category: chosen
    canfd_payload_32 = 32  # category: chosen
    canfd_baud_arb = 1.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: chosen
    canfd_baud_data = 5.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: chosen
    canfd_ifs = 6.0 * microsecond  # category: illustrative

    # EtherCAT parameters
    ethercat_payload_axis = 32  # category: chosen
    ethercat_baud = 100.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: datasheet (100BASE-TX link rate)
    ethercat_header = 64  # category: illustrative
    ethercat_hop = 0.6 * microsecond  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    canfd_64 = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(
        num_axes=num_axes,
        payload_bytes=canfd_payload_64,
        baud_arbitration=canfd_baud_arb,
        baud_data=canfd_baud_data,
        cycle_time=cycle_time,
        interframe_spacing=canfd_ifs,
    )
    canfd_32 = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(
        num_axes=num_axes,
        payload_bytes=canfd_payload_32,
        baud_arbitration=canfd_baud_arb,
        baud_data=canfd_baud_data,
        cycle_time=cycle_time,
        interframe_spacing=canfd_ifs,
    )
    ethercat = calc_ethercat_cycle_time(
        num_axes=num_axes,
        bytes_per_axis=ethercat_payload_axis,
        baud_rate=ethercat_baud,
        header_bytes=ethercat_header,
        hop_delay=ethercat_hop,
        cycle_time=cycle_time,
    )

    t_tx_canfd_64 = canfd_64["t_tx"]
    t_total_canfd_64 = canfd_64["t_total_tx"]
    rho_canfd_64 = canfd_64["utilization"]

    t_tx_canfd_32 = canfd_32["t_tx"]
    t_total_canfd_32 = canfd_32["t_total_tx"]
    rho_canfd_32 = canfd_32["utilization"]

    drive_axes = num_axes - arm_axes

    t_frame_ethercat = ethercat["t_tx"]
    t_hop_ethercat = ethercat["t_forward"]
    t_total_ethercat = ethercat["t_cycle_total"]
    t_margin_ethercat = ethercat["t_margin"]
    rho_ethercat = ethercat["utilization"]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_tx_canfd_64.to(microsecond).magnitude - 140.4) < 0.5, f"Unexpected CAN-FD 64B frame time: {t_tx_canfd_64}")
    check(num_axes == 9 and arm_axes == 7 and drive_axes == 2, f"Axis split drifted: {num_axes} = {arm_axes} + {drive_axes}")
    check(abs(cycle_time.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, f"Bus cycle drifted: {cycle_time}")
    check(abs(t_total_canfd_64.to(microsecond).magnitude - 1263.6) < 0.5, f"Unexpected CAN-FD 64B total: {t_total_canfd_64}")
    check(rho_canfd_64 > 1.0, "CAN-FD 64B must overrun 1.0 ms cycle time")
    check(abs(t_total_ethercat.to(microsecond).magnitude - 33.56) < 0.05, f"Unexpected EtherCAT total: {t_total_ethercat}")
    check(abs(t_margin_ethercat.to(microsecond).magnitude - 966.44) < 0.05, f"Unexpected unallocated bus time: {t_margin_ethercat}")
    check(rho_ethercat < 0.05, "EtherCAT utilization must be under 5%")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    num_axes_str = fmt_int(num_axes)
    arm_axes_str = fmt_int(arm_axes)
    drive_axes_str = fmt_int(drive_axes)
    cycle_time_str = fmt_latency(cycle_time, unit=millisecond, precision=0)

    t_tx_canfd_64_str = fmt_latency(t_tx_canfd_64, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_total_canfd_64_us_str = fmt_latency(t_total_canfd_64, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_total_canfd_64_ms_str = fmt_latency(t_total_canfd_64, unit=millisecond, precision=3)
    rho_canfd_64_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_canfd_64, precision=1)

    t_tx_canfd_32_str = fmt_latency(t_tx_canfd_32, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_total_canfd_32_str = fmt_latency(t_total_canfd_32, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_canfd_32_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_canfd_32, precision=1)

    t_frame_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_frame_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_hop_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_hop_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_total_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_total_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_margin_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_margin_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_ethercat_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_ethercat, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-nervous-fieldbus-serialization-latency-wcet-schedulability .callout-notebook title="Fieldbus serialization before schedulability"}
**Practical engineering question**: The mobile manipulator's permission path commands `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` servo axes, `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.arm_axes_str` arm joints and `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.drive_axes_str` drive wheels, once per `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.cycle_time_str` bus cycle. How much of that cycle do the listed CAN-FD frames or one EtherCAT frame occupy before controller and device delays are counted?

*1. CAN-FD Serialization and Arbitration Latency (`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` Axes, 64-byte payload per axis):*
- Bitrate: $1.0\text{ Mbps}$ arbitration phase, $5.0\text{ Mbps}$ data phase.
- Per-frame bit count: 32 bits arbitration/CRC overhead at $1.0\text{ Mbps}$ ($32\,\mu\text{s}$), 512 bits payload at $5.0\text{ Mbps}$ ($102.4\,\mu\text{s}$), plus inter-frame spacing $\approx 6.0\,\mu\text{s}$.
- Transmission time per axis: $t_{\text{tx}} \approx$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_tx_canfd_64_str`.
- For `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` axes polling cyclically: `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` $\times$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_tx_canfd_64_str` $=$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_canfd_64_us_str` ($=$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_canfd_64_ms_str`).
- Result: Bus utilization exceeds 100 percent ($\rho \approx$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_canfd_64_pct_str` $> 1.0$), so this schedule of `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` frames cannot fit a `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.cycle_time_str` bus cycle even before processing. If payload is reduced to 32 bytes ($t_{\text{tx}} \approx$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_tx_canfd_32_str`), total bus time is `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_canfd_32_str` (`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_canfd_32_pct_str` utilization). This reduced payload still needs arbitration, error/retransmission allowances, competing frames, and response-time analysis; no universal 70 percent utilization threshold establishes schedulability.

*2. EtherCAT On-The-Fly Processing (`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` Axes, Daisy-Chain Ring):*
- Bitrate: $100\text{ Mbps}$ full-duplex Fast Ethernet ($10\text{ ns/bit}$).
- A single standard Ethernet frame carries all `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` joint commands and sensor returns in one pass.
- Frame serialization time: `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_frame_ethercat_str`.
- Hardware forwarding mechanism: Dedicated EtherCAT peripheral node controller application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) (such as the Beckhoff ET1100) utilize internal hardware shift registers to extract commanded setpoints and insert sensor feedback on the fly as the physical Ethernet telegram traverses the node. Because the frame is never stored in a software buffer before retransmission, each physical peripheral node introduces only an internal silicon gate delay ($0.6\,\mu\text{s}$ per hop).
- Node forwarding delay: `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` peripheral ASIC controller hops at $0.6\,\mu\text{s}$ per hop $=$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_hop_ethercat_str`.
- Modeled frame serialization plus `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` forwarding hops: $T_{\text{bus}} =$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_frame_ethercat_str` $+$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_hop_ethercat_str` $=$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_ethercat_str`.
- Result: These modeled bus terms occupy `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_ethercat_pct_str` of the cycle, leaving `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_margin_ethercat_str` **unallocated by this bus calculation**. Coordinator/node processing, propagation, clock synchronization, retries, application computation, and actuator response still consume the end-to-end deadline.

**Systems insight**: For the machine's `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` axes at 64 bytes per axis, CAN-FD serialization alone misses the `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.cycle_time_str` bus cycle, while EtherCAT frame and forwarding occupancy leaves room for other work. In cyber-physical safety, every millisecond of bus latency or serialization delay adds directly to pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, consuming $v \cdot \Delta t_{\text{bus}}$ ($1.5\text{ mm}$ per millisecond at the drive limit) of stopping clearance. Worse, CAN-FD arbitration is non-preemptive: if an emergency stop command arrives while an unprivileged telemetry frame is transmitting, the brake command blocks for at least $140.4\,\mu\text{s}$, and retransmissions under electromagnetic noise compound this delay across multiple cycles. By circulating a single frame through hardware shift registers, EtherCAT confines bus transit to `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_ethercat_str`, guaranteeing that emergency braking commands reach drive inverters deterministically within the budgeted $T_{\text{bus}} =$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.cycle_time_str`. **TSN Ethernet**\index{Time-sensitive networking} can carry gigabit camera feeds and microsecond servo frames on one physical link, but only if its time-gated queues are configured and verified across every switch so that video bursts cannot collide with time-critical control slots.
:::

### Bandwidth and jitter trade-offs on the synchronization frontier {#sec-nervous-synchronization-frontier}

Real-time dependability cannot be achieved by buying faster clock speeds or measuring statistical latency percentiles on an idle bench. Dependability requires structural analysis of the execution path: eliminating all unbounded variance sources ($I_{\text{unbounded}} = 0$), bounding shared hardware blocking ($B$), enforcing zero-allocation static memory layouts, and selecting deterministic bus protocols with hardware distributed clocks (@fig-04-fieldbus-evolution).

While bandwidth determines how many bytes can cross the bus in a given interval, **synchronization jitter** ($\sigma_{\text{jitter}}$)—the worst-case temporal variation in when distributed nodes sample sensors and apply actuator setpoints—determines whether multi-axis physical systems can maintain stable dynamical contact. In multi-axis robotic arms and legged humanoids, field-oriented control (FOC) switches inverter pulse-width modulation (PWM) gates at $20\text{--}40\,\text{kHz}$, demanding sub-microsecond phase synchronization ($\le 1\,\mu\text{s}$) across all joint drives to prevent phase distortion, audible acoustic resonance, and destructive torque ripple. If inter-joint clock synchronization jitters by even tens of microseconds, distributed PWM carrier waves drift out of phase. When two drives actuate a stiff kinematic chain—such as two drive wheels maintaining heading or two arm joints holding a rigid workpiece—this inter-axis phase skew forces one motor to apply accelerating torque while the adjacent motor is still executing commutation on a previous phase angle, exciting high-frequency structural vibration and risking false overcurrent comparator trips.

As mapped across four decades of communication standards in @fig-04-fieldbus-evolution, robotic command transport has evolved through three distinct synchronization regimes:

- **Regime I (Soft real-time CSMA/CR arbitration, $0.2\text{--}20\,\text{ms}$ jitter):** Legacy serial protocols (Modbus RTU) and carrier-sense priority-arbitrated buses (CAN 2.0B, CAN-FD) exhibit millisecond-scale queuing jitter under high bus loads. In CAN, lower-priority frames must wait for an ongoing transmission to finish (non-preemptive blocking), while arbitration collisions and retransmissions introduce non-deterministic delays that restrict these networks to supervisory setpoints and low-rate telemetry.
- **Regime II (Coordinated multi-axis joint servos, $50\text{--}100\,\mu\text{s}$ jitter):** Switched Ethernet and static time-division multiple access (FlexRay, PROFINET RT) bridge the gap between supervisory CAN and microsecond fieldbuses. By partitioning transmission into deterministic time slots, Regime II networks achieve reliable $1\,\text{kHz}$ position control across multi-joint manipulators, though residual software protocol stack overhead and switch queuing jitter remain too large for direct inverter gate switching.
- **Regime III (Sub-microsecond physical AI synchronization, $< 1\,\mu\text{s}$ jitter):** Hardware-scheduled time-triggered architectures—specifically processing-on-the-fly real-time Ethernet with hardware Distributed Clocks (EtherCAT, EtherCAT G) and IEEE 802.1AS/Qbv Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)[^fn-net-tsn-fieldbus]—anchor clock alignment directly in physical layer (PHY) hardware timestamps. Dedicated Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) circuits or tapped-delay-line counters inside the PHY transceiver silicon latch timestamps at the exact physical arrival of the Start of Frame Delimiter (SFD), completely bypassing operating system interrupt latency, DMA buffering delays, and media access control (MAC) FIFO queuing jitter. By continuously measuring physical cable propagation delays ($t_{\text{prop}}$) and disciplining local node oscillators to sub-100 nanosecond precision via TDC timestamp capture, Regime III enables real-time controllers to align hardware `SYNC0` trigger pulses across all nodes within $\le 50\text{ ns}$, coordinating $20\text{--}40\,\text{kHz}$ PWM motor inverters across dozens of distributed axes without phase distortion.

[^fn-net-tsn-fieldbus]: **Time-Sensitive Networking**\index{Time-sensitive networking}: IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Sensitive Networking establishes deterministic Ethernet communication by configuring time-aware traffic shapers across network switches. High-priority control frames execute within dedicated, pre-scheduled transmission windows, while asynchronous high-bandwidth payloads (such as uncompressed camera streams) are temporarily gated. This scheduled time-division multiplexing allows vision telemetry and microsecond servo commands to coexist over a unified physical link without packet collision or buffer bloat.

::: {#fig-04-fieldbus-evolution fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The nervous system frontier: fieldbus bandwidth vs. clock synchronization jitter across industrial robotic protocols (1979–2026)**: Trade-off between raw transmission bandwidth (log scale, $100\\,\\text{kbps}$ to $10\\,\\text{Gbps}$) and worst-case synchronization jitter (log scale, $10\\,\\text{ns}$ to $20\\,\\text{ms}$). Regime I (top): Non-deterministic soft real-time protocols (Modbus RTU, CAN 2.0B, CAN-FD) subject to CSMA/CR collision arbitration and unmanaged queuing jitter ($0.2\\text{--}20\\,\\text{ms}$). Regime II (middle): Coordinated multi-axis joint servo loops ($1\\,\\text{kHz}$, jitter $\\le 100\\,\\mu\\text{s}$) utilizing switched Ethernet and static TDMA (FlexRay, PROFINET RT). Regime III (bottom): Sub-microsecond motor inverter and physical AI synchronization frontier (EtherCAT, EtherCAT G, IEEE TSN 802.1AS/Qbv), achieving sub-100 ns clock alignment via hardware distributed clocks and processing-on-the-fly forwarding to eliminate torque ripple during $20\\text{--}40\\,\\text{kHz}$ PWM field-oriented control." fig-alt="Log-log plot of fieldbus raw bandwidth from 0.05 Mbps to 25 Gbps on the horizontal axis against worst-case synchronization jitter from 10 ns to 50 ms on the vertical axis. Three distinct shaded regions demarcate soft real-time CSMA protocols, 1 kHz coordinated joint servo protocols, and sub-microsecond hardware-synchronized EtherCAT and TSN fabrics. Specific milestones from 1979 Modbus to 2024 TSN highlight bandwidth gains and jitter reductions."}
