```{python}
    add_badge(ax, p["text"], xy=(p["bw"], p["jitter"]), xytext=p["badge_xytext"], color="#1E293B", fontsize=7.8, arrow=True, arrow_color=p["color"])

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")

ax.set_xlim(0.05, 25000.0)
ax.set_ylim(0.006, 50000.0)

ax.yaxis.set_minor_locator(ticker.NullLocator())

ax.set_xticks([0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1000.0, 10000.0])
ax.get_xaxis().set_major_formatter(
    ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, p: f"{int(x*1000)} kbps" if x < 1.0 else (f"{int(x)} Mbps" if x < 1000.0 else f"{int(x/1000)} Gbps"))
)

ax.set_yticks([0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1000.0, 10000.0])
ax.get_yaxis().set_major_formatter(
    ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda y, p: f"{int(y*1000)} ns" if y < 1.0 else (f"{int(y)} µs" if y < 1000.0 else f"{int(y/1000)} ms"))
)

ax.set_xlabel("Fieldbus Raw Bandwidth / Bitrate (log scale)", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", labelpad=8)
ax.set_ylabel(
    "Worst-Case Clock Synchronization Jitter (log scale)  [ $\\downarrow$ Lower Jitter = Higher Determinism ]",
    fontsize=10.5,
    fontweight="bold",
    labelpad=8,
)

legend_elements = [
    Line2D([0], [0], marker='s', color='w', markerfacecolor='#475569', markersize=8, label='Serial Master-Slave (Modbus RS-485)'),
    Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markerfacecolor='#A51C30', markersize=8, label='Asynchronous CSMA/CR (CAN, CAN-FD)'),
    Line2D([0], [0], marker='^', color='w', markerfacecolor='#008080', markersize=8, label='Time-Triggered Static TDMA (FlexRay)'),
    Line2D(
        [0], [0], marker='D', color='w', markerfacecolor='#B45309', markersize=8, label='Switched / Isochronous Industrial Ethernet (PROFINET RT/IRT)'
    ),
    Line2D([0], [0], marker='*', color='w', markerfacecolor='#1E793C', markersize=12, label='On-the-Fly & Converged TSN (EtherCAT, TSN 802.1AS/Qbv)'),
]
legend = ax.legend(
    handles=legend_elements,
    loc="upper right",
    frameon=True,
    framealpha=0.96,
    edgecolor="#CBD5E1",
    fontsize=7.8,
    title="Industrial Fieldbus Architectures",
    title_fontsize=8.2,
)
legend.get_title().set_fontweight("bold")
legend.set_zorder(15)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.subplots_adjust(top=0.95, bottom=0.10, left=0.08, right=0.94)
plt.show()
```

:::

A bounded path delivers each command to the drives within its cycle, but it is indifferent to which commands it carries. Which processor may place a command on that path, and what that processor must check first, is a question of authority rather than timing.

## Actuation Authority {#sec-nervous-actuation-authority}

Authority on the mobile manipulator is the physical ability to write the drive registers that energize its base and arm windings and deliver mechanical power. In modern operating systems, hardware memory management units (MMUs) and execution rings (such as x86 Ring 0 kernel mode versus Ring 3 user mode, or ARM Exception Levels EL1 versus EL0) enforce process isolation: an unprivileged user application cannot execute privileged CPU instructions or directly mutate page tables. In physical AI architectures, actuation authority establishes the cyber-physical equivalent of hardware privilege separation.

In an embodied machine, allowing complex, uncertified perception and planning software to write actuator control registers directly is a fatal architectural anti-pattern. A learned foundation model or trajectory planner on an application processor must run in an unprivileged domain (Ring 3), possessing zero physical authority to write PWM timer registers (`TIMx_CCR`), set gate-driver current references, or toggle motor bridge enable pins that govern current delivery to stator windings. Instead, high-level software generates unprivileged trajectory proposals ($p_t$). These proposals pass across an isolated memory transport interface into a deterministic safety microcontroller operating as the privileged supervisor (Ring 0). As contrasted in @fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers, decoupling proposal generation from physical execution privilege ensures that a software crash, kernel panic, or runaway GPU kernel cannot command unverified torque to the motors.

::: {#fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Hardware proposal boundary**: (a) Decoupled enforcer on an isolated safety microcontroller with exclusive write privilege over motor drive registers, while the host processor proposes trajectories across a shared-memory link. (b) Collapsed unsafe architecture where unverified host software writes actuator registers directly, creating a single failure domain." fig-alt="Comparison of hardware privilege architectures: (a) Decoupled real-time enforcer gating actuator registers with a separate torque-cutoff trip branch; (b) Unsafe collapsed architecture with direct unchecked writes from host to motor registers."}
![](images/svg/fig04_privilege_enforcer_registers.svg){width="90%"}
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Actuator override masking registers implement the hardware preemption tiers formulated in @sec-intervention-authority-log.
:::

The microcontroller continuously evaluates physical safety invariants: verifying that commanded joint positions lie within physical reach envelopes, that joint velocities do not exceed certified limits, and that projected decelerations remain safely within dynamic stopping clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$). If a proposal satisfies all invariants, the microcontroller grants execution permission, interpolates waypoints into high-frequency current references ($u_t$), and writes to the physical gate-driver registers. If a proposal is invalid or expired, the enforcer revokes permission ($\bot$) and requests a controlled deceleration or hold. A separate hardware trip zone can remove drive torque on a fault; opening switches does not itself brake moving mass.[^fn-hw-tripzone-break]

[^fn-hw-tripzone-break]: **Hardware Trip Zone**\index{Hardware trip zone}: Microcontroller hardware trip zones (such as TI `EPWM_TZFRC` or STM32 `TIMx_BDTR` Break inputs) couple analog overcurrent and overvoltage comparators directly to timer output logic. Upon fault detection, configured trip logic may force gate signals high-impedance or activate a validated braking mode. These have different mechanical consequences: torque removal can leave the plant coasting, while dynamic braking requires a rated energy path.

When safety limits are breached, physical AI systems must distinguish between controlled stopping and torque removal under IEC 60204-1 stop categories:

- **Stop Category 0 (Immediate Torque Removal / Safe Torque Off):** Actuator power is cut immediately, forcing motor inverter switches into an open, high-impedance state. While this guarantees that software cannot drive current into the motor, torque removal does not actively decelerate the robot. Crucially, on gravity-loaded vertical joints or high-speed mobile bases, an uncontrolled Stop Category 0 lets moving mass coast freely or crash downward under gravitational acceleration unless spring-applied electromechanical holding brakes mechanically clamp the rotor shafts.
- **Stop Category 1 (Controlled Deceleration with Delayed STO):** Power remains applied to the actuators to drive an active, coordinated braking deceleration profile down to zero velocity. Once the mechanism is fully halted, Safe Torque Off (STO) engages and mechanical holding brakes clamp.
- **Stop Category 2 (Controlled Stop with Power Maintained):** Actuators execute active deceleration to zero velocity, after which drive power remains continuously energized to hold position under closed-loop torque control.

The refusal carries its own physical cost. If the enforcer rejects an invalid proposal and commands dynamic braking on a fast-moving joint, the braking path must have enough torque, clearance, and thermal capacity to arrest the mass.[^fn-math-braking-dynamics] Over a braking interval of hundreds of milliseconds, the winding resistance, brake resistor, or friction that forms that path must absorb the joint's kinetic energy within the thermal limits of @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles, without damaging the winding insulation or letting the mass coast past its clearance.

[^fn-math-braking-dynamics]: **Braking Dynamics**\index{Braking dynamics}: Arresting a high-inertia manipulator joint transfers kinetic energy into the implemented braking path: winding and power electronics losses, a rated brake resistor, or mechanical friction. The trajectory must satisfy stopping clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$) and each component's pulse-energy and thermal limits; $\int I^2R\,dt$ accounts for the winding share when resistive motor braking is used. For the complete derivation of kinematic stopping envelopes and transient thermal dissipation, see @sec-appendix-control.

By virtue of the causal boundary established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, the enforcer treats the origin of an aberrant proposal as irrelevant. A remote memory exploit in an operating system daemon, an adversarial camera perturbation inducing model hallucination, and an arithmetic overflow in a neural matrix multiplier all produce the same boundary event, an invalid proposal packet. Because the enforcer evaluates invariant bounds against physical sensor feedback from optical encoders and current shunts rather than inspecting neural network weights, it needs no model of why a proposal went wrong, and the host, which cannot write actuator registers directly, has no path around it. Protection against a compromised host still depends on independent sensing, a correct limit model, actuator capability, and a feasible fallback.

To guard against internal hardware faults or microcontroller latch-ups within the enforcer itself, the system incorporates out-of-band supervisory channels and physical disconnects. These channels consist of unprogrammable analog circuits, hardwired emergency stop mushroom push buttons, and dual-channel safety relays that sever power to the motor inverter bridges independently of all digital logic through Safe Torque Off (@fig-real-estop, IEC 61800-5-2), which physically interrupts gate-driver bias to prevent torque-producing stator current.[^fn-std-iec61800-sto] These disconnects cost availability. Re-energizing a tripped high-voltage DC bus requires pre-charging the inverter filter capacitors through current-limiting resistors, because closing the contactor onto empty capacitors draws an inrush large enough to weld its contacts, and the pre-charge takes hundreds of milliseconds before motor control can resume. A disconnect therefore trades availability and active control for a fault response whose mechanical consequences depend on brakes, load, and stored energy, and it can act when the primary controller fails only if it shares no hidden clock, power rail, or silicon with that controller.

[^fn-std-iec61800-sto]: **Safe Torque Off (STO)**\index{Safe torque off}: An STO implementation removes torque-producing drive signals through a hardware interlock. An IEC 61800-5-2 integrity rating depends on the actual devices, diagnostic coverage, wiring, and validation, not on the circuit pattern alone.

::: {#fig-real-estop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path**: A dual-channel emergency switch and monitored relays remove torque-producing gate bias; a separate spring-applied holding brake is shown. This diagram describes a hardware response path, not a certified integrity level or proof of stopping distance (synthesized from ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2)." fig-alt="Four-stage out-of-band safety interlock schematic: Dual-channel positive-break E-stop, force-guided safety relays with EDM feedback, gate bias cutoff with holding brake, and motor plant de-energized to zero torque."}
![](images/svg/fig04_sto_safety_circuit.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The hardware interlock shown in @fig-real-estop executes this protection across four discrete stages:

1. *Stage 1 (Dual-channel positive-break input):* An emergency stop mushroom pushbutton incorporates dual normally closed contacts. Depressing the actuator mechanically forces both contact sets open, even in the presence of contact welding.
2. *Stage 2 (Monitored safety relays with EDM):* Redundant force-guided safety relays cross-check both contact channels and monitor relay state via External Device Monitoring (EDM) feedback. Any channel discordance (such as a cut wire or welded contact) permanently prevents circuit reset.
3. *Stage 3 (Optocoupled gate-bias cutoff):* Opening the safety relays severs the power rail feeding the optocouplers that supply gate-bias voltage ($+15\,\text{V}$) to the motor inverter gate drivers. Without gate bias, the high-side and low-side power switches remain in an open, high-impedance state, physically preventing torque generation regardless of software PWM commands.
4. *Stage 4 (Spring-applied holding brake engagement):* De-energizing the circuit simultaneously cuts current to an electromechanical holding brake solenoid, allowing mechanical springs to clamp friction pads against the motor shaft and arrest rotating inertia.

::: {#psp-nervous-hardware-authority .callout-perspective title="Hardware authority invariant"}
If an unverified learned policy has direct memory-mapped write access to actuator gate-driver registers, the machine has no safety layer, and its next out-of-distribution input reaches the motors unchecked.
:::

Write privilege is therefore a physical fact about wires and registers, not a software permission, and the Brain holds none of it. That privilege protects the plant only while the enforcer stays independent of the processor whose proposals it refuses. If the two share a clock, a rail, or a memory bus, a fault in the proposer can silence the enforcer without ever writing to a drive.

## Hardware Isolation {#sec-nervous-hardware-isolation}

Independence between the application processor and the permission path is a claim that often fails its first verification. In server-side machine learning infrastructure, multi-tenant workloads are considered isolated when encapsulated in software abstractions—such as Linux cgroups, Docker containers, or virtual machine hypervisors. In cyber-physical AI systems, however, **software virtualization is an architectural illusion of isolation**. Virtual partitions share the same physical silicon substrate, memory interconnect, power distribution network (PDN), and clock distribution trees. A software exception in a containerized vision daemon cannot breach memory protection directly, but an accelerator power spike or memory bus sweep executed by that daemon immediately propagates across shared physical hardware channels.

Verifying true fault-domain independence requires proving physical isolation across four distinct hardware dimensions: independent execution silicon with private instruction pipelines, separate timing references from segregated crystal oscillators, isolated power rails from independent regulators, and segregated memory domains without shared dynamic random-access memory chips or interconnect arbitration buses.[^fn-std-iso26262-ffi] Any shared substrate needs a formal common-cause fault analysis demonstrating that failure in the unprivileged deliberative domain cannot compromise the cycle-deterministic execution of the independent permission path.

[^fn-std-iso26262-ffi]: **Freedom from Interference (FFI)**\index{Freedom from interference}: ISO 26262-9 and IEC 61508 formalize Freedom from Interference (FFI) as the absence of cascading faults between software elements possessing different safety integrity levels. Unverified neural policies sharing silicon or bus fabrics with safety-critical tasks require architects to demonstrate spatial (memory protection), temporal (independent scheduling and timers), and electrical isolation (independent power rails). Shared resources require evidence that interference cannot defeat the specified enforcement deadlines and fault response.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-permission-rail
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SHARED CONTROL RAIL VS. THE HELD-UP PERMISSION RAIL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation, the shared-infrastructure paragraph.
# │ Goal:    Name the rail the application processor shares and the isolated,
# │          held-up rail the permission path runs on instead.
# │ Show:    24 V shared control rail, 18 V regulator dropout, 2 s hold-up.
# │ How:     Registry fields on RM; the sag below the dropout is derived in
# │          @sec-body-power-integrity, and the hold-up is sized in
# │          @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_voltage, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PermissionRail:
    """The permission path's isolated, held-up rail beside the shared control rail."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_rail = RM.control_rail_nominal  # category: chosen (shared 24 V control rail)
    v_dropout = RM.control_rail_dropout  # category: illustrative (regulator dropout)
    t_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen (permission-rail hold-up)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_headroom = (v_rail - v_dropout).to(volt)  # headroom a full-charge rail starts with

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_rail.to(volt).magnitude - 24.0) < 1e-9, f"Control rail drifted: {v_rail}")
    check(abs(v_dropout.to(volt).magnitude - 18.0) < 1e-9, f"Regulator dropout drifted: {v_dropout}")
    check(abs(t_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Permission-rail hold-up drifted: {t_holdup}")
    check(v_headroom.magnitude > 0, "The shared rail must start above its regulator dropout")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_rail_str = fmt_voltage(v_rail, unit=volt, precision=0)
    v_dropout_str = fmt_voltage(v_dropout, unit=volt, precision=0)
    t_holdup_str = fmt_latency(t_holdup, unit=second, precision=0)
```

Shared electrical and physical infrastructure creates cross-domain failure modes that bypass all software access controls. On the mobile manipulator, the application processor and the permission path share a primary battery but not a power rail. When drive motors accelerate under peak torque or GPU accelerators launch sudden inference bursts, transient current draws can sag the shared `{python} PermissionRail.v_rail_str` control rail below its regulators' `{python} PermissionRail.v_dropout_str` dropout threshold (@sec-body-power-integrity), causing unisolated processors to brown out and reset. If the safety microcontroller shared that unisolated rail, a brownout would float its GPIO lines to high impedance during reboot; floating gate-driver pins risk destructive shoot-through across inverter MOSFETs or leave the machine's moving kinetic momentum ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$) coasting uncontrolled through clearance. To eliminate this hazard, the permission path runs on the isolated rail of @sec-body-archetype-matrix, held up with diode-isolated storage capacitors for `{python} PermissionRail.t_holdup_str`. While the application processor reboots in the dark, the safety microcontroller rides through the transient, receives the brownout as an undervoltage flag, orchestrates an active Stop Category 1 deceleration or trips Safe Torque Off, engages mechanical holding brakes, and safely arrests the plant before logic power ever degrades.

On a shared silicon package or common thermal heat sink, sustained computational load on the application processor elevates junction temperatures beyond $105^\circ\text{C}$, triggering thermal throttling or silicon shutdown in adjacent real-time cores. When communication relies on an arbitrated interface such as a shared peripheral interconnect or memory bus, a high-bandwidth visual pipeline or a misbehaving direct memory access controller can saturate bus bandwidth, starving the permission path of encoder feedback and sensor telemetry. Even a common clock oscillator creates an unbudgeted single point of failure, where thermal drift, mechanical vibration, or crystal cracking desynchronizes both domains at the same instant.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_substrate_blast_radius.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Blast radius diagram showing a compute and drive transient sagging the shared control rail, with thermal coupling, DMA starvation, and clock jitter spreading across a shared substrate, and the sag stopping at the isolated, held-up permission rail."}

*A transient on the shared rail reaches every load that draws from it; the permission path rides through on its own isolated, held-up rail.*
:::

The permission path must distinguish two failure modes of the proposer, unresponsiveness and corruption. Unresponsiveness occurs when an inference pipeline hangs, a scheduling deadline is missed, or operating system memory fragmentation blocks execution, producing no output. The permission path detects it through the heartbeat of @sec-nervous-cadences, which the application processor must deliver across an isolated channel before its timeout.

Corruption occurs when the proposer remains fully active and passes its heartbeat deadline, but generates kinematically impossible setpoints, discontinuous velocity requests, or numerical infinities resulting from out-of-distribution visual inputs or matrix overflow. The enforcer answers the two failures through separate mechanisms. A missing fresh chunk or a missed heartbeat revokes the proposal when its timer expires, whereas corruption triggers an immediate invariant rejection on the arrival of the malformed proposal packet.

The chunk lease is distinct from the host heartbeat. When the application processor stays alive but stops publishing admissible chunks, the drives would otherwise keep tracking the last admitted setpoints, and the machine would keep moving under a proposal that nothing has renewed, until the enforcer detects the expiry and begins deceleration. Enforcing the lease at the causal boundary (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary) bounds that interval. On the mobile manipulator, @sec-nervous-cadences sized that interval as a term of the stopping budget and charged it against the pre-brake ceiling.[^fn-math-watchdog-lease] The heartbeat can report that the process is alive, but it cannot renew an expired chunk, and its period is independent of the proposer's. Only the chunk policy renews often enough to hold the lease, and @sec-nervous-coupled-budget shows why the intent model cannot.

[^fn-math-watchdog-lease]: **Chunk Lease Bound**\index{Watchdog lease!bound}: For a constant-speed approach, the chunk lease, the tick, the bus cycle, and brake onset must satisfy the pre-brake inequality of @sec-nervous-cadences once the observation age $t_{\text{age}}$ joins them on the left side, and a post-expiry hold $T_{\text{hold}}$ adds to that side as well. The right-hand side is the pre-brake ceiling, not a lease to spend in full. For the complete algebraic derivation of lease bounds under bounded deceleration, see @sec-appendix-control-teleop-leases.

A timer feed proves only that the feed path ran. In *Bookout v. Toyota* (2013), a plaintiff expert argued that a timer-tick interrupt kept servicing the watchdog while other tasks could die [@barr2013toyota]; this is a reported trial mechanism, not a finding that electronic faults caused unintended acceleration in every investigated vehicle.

When a lease expires or an enforcer rejects a corrupted proposal, the permission path executes an explicit degradation strategy rather than an unconditioned power cut, because cutting power hands a moving actuator to whichever unpowered state its drive falls into (@sec-body-power-integrity), and none of those states is a controlled stop. Degradation follows a deterministic state hierarchy calculated within the permission path. An optional short continuation of the last validated trajectory is permissible only while its chunk lease remains valid and its stopping margin is feasible. After expiry, any further hold or dead reckoning $T_{\text{hold}}$ enters $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ and must fit in the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_left_str` of pre-brake ceiling that the lease path and brake onset leave at the drive limit (\ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}); the enforcer must begin braking sooner if the measured bounds of the remaining terms do not fit. If communication does not resume within that budget, the permission path requests controlled deceleration using the available torque and thermal budget established in @sec-body-actuator-limits. It reaches rest only if clearance and braking capability remain sufficient. A gravity-loaded arm may require a rated mechanical holding brake after motion has been arrested.

Once the physical plant is brought to a complete, stationary halt, the architecture executes a **recovery handshake**\index{Recovery handshake} before restoring autonomous proposal authority. The safety microcontroller asserts a persistent `FAULT_HELD` latch in a status word it owns and reports the exact physical rest pose $(\mathbf{q}_{\text{rest}}, \dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{0})$. The application processor must flush its stale action chunks, clear its autoregressive key-value (KV) attention cache, re-ingest fresh optical observations tagged with new hardware timestamps, and publish a re-synchronized chunk proposal.

Flushing the autoregressive key-value (KV) attention cache during the recovery handshake is an essential physical AI requirement. If an autoregressive policy or vision-language-action model preserves its pre-fault KV cache tokens, the transformer conditions subsequent token generation on historical trajectory states that preceded the emergency stop. The model then hallucinates continuity with where the robot was before the fault, emitting action chunk setpoints with a severe spatial discontinuity relative to the physical rest pose $\mathbf{q}_{\text{rest}}$. This sudden step command demands impossible joint accelerations, inducing an instantaneous torque spike that immediately re-trips the enforcer's kinematic invariants and locks the robot in an unrecoverable fault-restart loop. Clearing the KV cache forces the neural policy to re-attend over fresh, verified sensory observations corresponding strictly to the stationary rest state. The microcontroller verifies that the initial waypoint of the new proposal matches the physical rest state within a strict spatial epsilon ($||\mathbf{a}_0 - \mathbf{q}_{\text{rest}}|| \le \epsilon_{\text{sync}}$) before releasing the fault latch and re-energizing pulse-width modulation (PWM) to the motor drives.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Real-time bus fault-recovery state machines are verified via hardware fault-injection in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

Verifying that these isolation boundaries function as designed requires physical falsification on the test bench. Four specific fault-injection regimes must be executed against the physical prototype: power-rail droop testing (injecting maximum-slew current steps to verify less than $50\text{ mV}$ of rail cross-coupling noise), clock glitching (verifying independent timing domains maintain stable cycle counts under frequency drift), communication bus flooding (saturating links to verify heartbeat telemetry retains deterministic transmission slots),[^fn-hw-canfd-arbitration] and numerical fault injection (streaming synthetic proposals containing NaNs and infinite floats to verify single-cycle rejection without execution stalls).

[^fn-hw-canfd-arbitration]: **CAN Arbitration**\index{CAN arbitration}: Controller Area Network protocols resolve bus contention at the physical layer using wired-AND dominant ('0') and recessive ('1') signaling. If a defective transceiver continuously asserts a dominant state (a "babbling idiot" fault), it monopolizes the shared physical bus and blocks all higher-level communication. Hardware bus guardians and dominant-timeout clamp circuits monitor transmission duration, physically disconnecting jabbering nodes to preserve network availability for remaining safety participants.

Independence is therefore validated against identified common-cause faults rather than read off a block diagram, and the lease that bounds a stopped proposer comes from the stopping margin that remains after detection and actuation delays. Both defenses bound a proposer that stops or fails, which leaves open whether a proposer running at the enforcer's own rate still needs a separate check.

## Invariant Checking {#sec-nervous-invariant-checking}

Locomotion policies and compact visuomotor models compiled for edge accelerators can emit a new actuator command every $2.0\text{ ms}$, which tempts designers to let the policy write the motor registers directly. Rate matching does not confer authority. A neural network emitting torques at $500\text{ Hz}$ is governed by the same statistical uncertainty as a large model generating waypoints at $5\text{ Hz}$, and even when policy and enforcer share one $2.0\text{ ms}$ period, the network's output remains a proposal that must pass the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model before it changes current in a winding.

Placing an unverified policy inside the fast loop exposes the plant to three classical systems failure modes:

1. *Compute underrun:* Occurs when tail latency jitter pushes an inference pass beyond the actuation deadline ($t_{\text{infer}} > D_i$), leaving the motor inverter without a fresh setpoint unless a deterministic default is latched.
2. *Out-of-distribution torque spikes:* Occurs when an adversarial visual input or unseen physical contact state produces an instantaneous, discontinuous torque reversal within a single cycle.
3. *Structural limit cycling:* Occurs when unmodeled gearbox compliance or sensor phase lag couples with high-gain neural policy feedback into self-excited limit-cycle resonance.

In distributed networking systems, in-line packet firewalls (such as kernel-level eBPF filters) inspect network packets at line rate, dropping or rewriting malformed packets in bounded $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time before they reach application sockets. In physical AI, the safety microcontroller acts as a **deterministic in-line packet firewall for physical actuation**. Operating within a microsecond execution budget inside tightly coupled memory (TCM/SRAM), the enforcer inspects every candidate proposal through a three-stage pre-actuation intervention pipeline:

1. *Stage 1 (Kinematic boundary clamping):* The enforcer projects commanded joint positions and velocities against certified kinematic limits, clamping setpoints that exceed workspace envelopes ($\mathbf{q} \in [\mathbf{q}_{\min}, \mathbf{q}_{\max}]$) or velocity ceilings ($|\dot{\mathbf{q}}| \le \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\max}$).
2. *Stage 2 (Rate-of-change torque limiter):* To prevent high-frequency current spikes that stress motor drive inverters and excite unmodeled structural resonances, the enforcer bounds torque slew: $|\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}| = |(\boldsymbol{\tau}_k - \boldsymbol{\tau}_{k-1})/\Delta t| \le \dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{\max}$. Commands exceeding the maximum allowable rate of torque change are rate-limited to preserve drive thermal margins and prevent mechanical shock.
3. *Stage 3 (Passivity energy observer):* The enforcer maintains a virtual energy tank that monitors the cumulative energy exchanged between the controller and the physical plant ($\int \boldsymbol{\tau}^T \dot{\mathbf{q}}\,dt$). If out-of-distribution neural policy chattering begins injecting non-passive energy into high-frequency structural modes, the passivity observer detects the energy surplus and immediately injects virtual damping or transitions the machine to a safe holding state before destructive resonance occurs (@sec-appendix-control-passivity).

Under deadline misses or compute underruns, the firewall does not stall or spin: it drops the late proposal in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time, evaluates remaining lease clearance, and executes a certified stopping suffix.

The same reasoning covers the one proposer that is not learned. A remote operator is a third proposer. Its commands pass the same permission path, and network delay spends the same pre-brake budget (@sec-intervention-human-authority). Neither speed nor a human origin gives a proposal authority; only passing the permission path's checks does, and each check spends part of a budget that the next section lays out handoff by handoff.

::: {#chk-nervous-hardware-invariants .callout-checkpoint title="Hardware isolation and invariant checking"}

Before turning to the handoffs between proposer and actuator, verify your understanding of the exchange, hardware isolation, and pre-actuation invariant defenses:

- [ ] **Nonblocking exchange**: Can you explain how the seqlock reader detects a torn read in one bounded attempt, and why a writer stopped mid-write leaves the active spline valid only until its lease expires?
- [ ] **Four dimensions of physical isolation**: Can you enumerate the four physical boundaries (silicon pipelines, timing crystals, power rails, memory buses) that a check for fault-domain independence must cover, and explain how shared paths would need validation?
- [ ] **Physical derivation of chunk leases**: Can you explain why the chunk lease must be sized from stopping distance and clearance rather than chosen as a software timeout, and why a heartbeat never renews it?
- [ ] **Rate matching and authority**: Can you explain why a policy that runs at the plant's own rate still produces only proposals, and which check answers each of its three failure modes?

:::

## The Handoffs Matrix {#sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix}

When the mobile manipulator overruns a stop, the diagnosis starts by locating the fault at one of five canonical handoffs between the photons its cameras collect and the current its drives deliver. In distributed systems engineering, microservices communicate across typed interface contracts governed by service-level objectives (SLOs)—such as target $P_{99}$ request latencies, network throughput allocations, and error budgets. In cloud environments, these are soft contracts: when a microservice violates an SLO, the distributed runtime absorbs the error via exponential-backoff retries, request rerouting, circuit breaking, or degraded response modes. In physical AI architectures, however, the five canonical handoffs define **hard cyber-physical service-level objectives**. Because software cannot recall moving kinetic momentum or undo thermal copper heating, an unbudgeted interface violation cannot be masked by software retries.

Upstream, sensing transfers raw transducer signals to perception pipelines. Perception yields intermediate representations that fuse into an estimated world state. The state feeds the learned policy to produce an action plan. The plan submits candidate trajectories to the safety enforcer. Finally, the approved command passes from the enforcer to the physical actuators. Across each boundary, five interface limits govern feasibility: latency ($\tau$), bandwidth ($\beta$), energy and heat ($\mathcal{E}$), determinism ($\sigma_t$), and fault domain isolation ($\mathcal{F}$). The five handoffs and the five interface limits form a five-by-five matrix that maps every signal path to the physical budgets of the machine. The limits are distinct from the body's five budgets of @sec-body-five-budgets, which enter the matrix chiefly through its latency and energy columns. The record this section produces, the **Transport Budget** (formalized on the machine as the **handoff record**\index{Transport budget!contract}\index{Handoff record}), consumes the Limit Record of @sec-body-measuring-limits and the Proposal Record of @sec-brain, which specifies proposer latency, renewal frequency, and evidence age in the same structural format.

The example allocation in @tbl-04-synthesis-grid marks which limits are design-limiting at each handoff, and its numbers are chosen budgets, not measurements. The matrix gathers the budgets of all three Part I chapters, together with the sensor capture that @sec-boundary-machine-model places at the Boundary. In the Boundary row ($\mathcal{H}_1$), where the world becomes measurement, bandwidth and latency bind first, because raw multi-camera pixels stream over SerDes lanes and the exposure window sets a floor on image age before serialization begins. The Brain rows ($\mathcal{H}_2$, $\mathcal{H}_3$) bind first on energy and latency, the inference costs that @sec-brain established. The Body row ($\mathcal{H}_5$) binds first on determinism and heat, because the current loops of @sec-body must run on time and every ampere they deliver warms the windings and the power stage.

The Nervous System row ($\mathcal{H}_4$) is the architectural bridge that ties the Brain and the Body together. The proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model) between the learned planner and the enforcer carries an action proposal ($p_t$), which consists of a compact spline parameterization or waypoint chunk. For the compact payload assumed in this grid, $\beta < 100\text{ kB/s}$ is budgeted, so bandwidth does not bind at this boundary; latency, determinism ($\sigma_t$), and fault domain isolation ($\mathcal{F}$) do. The permission path isolates stochastic proposals with nonblocking mailboxes and expiring leases. On the mobile manipulator the latency limit is the chunk lease, which takes `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` of the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_str` pre-brake ceiling at the drive limit (@sec-nervous-cadences), and each chunk is admitted or refused within one `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` permission tick. Isolation rests on a private bus, a separate oscillator, and the isolated, held-up rail of @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation.

From the causal boundary perspective framed in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, when a physical AI system fails, the breakdown manifests as an unbudgeted limit crossing at a specific handoff cell rather than an abstract deficiency in learned intelligence. When diagnosing an over-budget stop, trajectory overrun, or subsystem fault, engineers walk @tbl-04-synthesis-grid through a three-step operational root-cause procedure:

1. *Locate the boundary seam:* Identify which physical handoff ($\mathcal{H}_1\text{--}\mathcal{H}_5$) recorded the initial timing excursion, sequence gap, torn payload, or thermal trip.
2. *Check the binding dimension:* Query the specific physical limit ($\tau, \beta, \mathcal{E}, \sigma_t, \mathcal{F}$) designated as *BINDING* for that handoff cell, which dictates the resource bottleneck governing the interface.
3. *Evaluate like-for-like evidence:* Compare runtime diagnostic traces directly against the certified bound kind (`requirement`, `proven bound`, or `measured distribution`), verifying whether the failure stemmed from an unmodeled microarchitectural tail event or a physical budget violation.

A handoff diagnosis must compare like evidence. For the $\mathcal{H}_2$ state-estimation path, suppose engineers allocate a $30.0\text{ ms}$ latency budget and measure $P_{99}=24.5\text{ ms}$ on a baseline hardware-in-the-loop run, a sampled margin of $+5.5\text{ ms}$. After thermal throttling, a measured $P_{99}=85.0\text{ ms}$ gives $-55.0\text{ ms}$ against that design budget. The decision is to reduce or reallocate workload and retain independent enforcement while revalidating. A $P_{99}$ sample diagnoses the regression; it is not a worst-case timing proof.

| Canonical Handoff Boundary                                  | Latency Limit ($\tau$)                                                                                                                                                                                            | Bandwidth Limit ($\beta$)                                                                                | Energy & Heat Limit ($\mathcal{E}$)                                                                 | Determinism Limit ($\sigma_t$)                                                                     | Fault Domain Isolation ($\mathcal{F}$)                                                          |
|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\mathcal{H}_1$: Sensing $\to$ Perception** *(Boundary)*  | **BINDING** \newline $\tau \le 16.7\text{ ms}$ (exposure & readout sets sensor age)                                                                                                                               | **BINDING** \newline $\beta \ge 1.2\text{ GB/s}$ (multi-camera 4K uncompressed streams)                  | *Non-binding* \newline $P < 3\text{ W}$ (sensor head dissipation isolated)                          | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t \le 1.0\text{ ms}$ (frame-sync triggers prevent skew)               | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by SerDes hardware & DMA ring buffers                           |
| **$\mathcal{H}_2$: Perception $\to$ State** *(Brain)*       | **BINDING** \newline $\tau \le 30.0\text{ ms}$ (visual-inertial odometry & feature window)                                                                                                                        | *Non-binding* \newline $\beta \approx 10\text{--}50\text{ MB/s}$ (compressed keypoints & voxels)         | **BINDING** \newline $P \approx 15\text{--}35\text{ W}$ (edge vision backbone accelerator envelope) | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by sliding-window state estimator buffers                          | **BINDING** \newline Spatial memory isolation: MPUs prevent memory corruption                   |
| **$\mathcal{H}_3$: State $\to$ Plan** *(Brain)*             | **BINDING** \newline $\tau \le 100.0\text{ ms}$ (autoregressive tokenization & diffusion horizon)                                                                                                                 | *Non-binding* \newline $\beta < 5\text{ MB/s}$ (low-dimensional state & prompt embeddings)               | **BINDING** \newline $P \approx 30\text{--}75\text{ W}$ (transformer/diffusion matrix accelerators) | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by receding-horizon chunking & spline buffers                      | **BINDING** \newline Sandboxed policy container prevents host panics halting telemetry          |
| **$\mathcal{H}_4$: Plan $\to$ Enforcer** *(Nervous System)* | **BINDING** \newline chunk lease `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` (chosen, inside limits derived from the stopping budget); per-tick admission within each `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` tick | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by compact parameterized splines ($\beta < 100\text{ kB/s}$)             | *Non-binding* \newline $P < 0.5\text{ W}$ (fixed-point constraint evaluation on MCU)                | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t \le 100\,\mu\text{s}$ (cycle-deterministic packet reception on MCU) | **BINDING** \newline Hardware boundary: private bus, separate oscillator, isolated held-up rail |
| **$\mathcal{H}_5$: Enforcer $\to$ Actuator** *(Body)*       | **BINDING** \newline $\tau \le 1.0\text{ ms}$ (servo interval $1.0\text{ ms}$; PWM loop $50\,\mu\text{s}$)                                                                                                        | *Non-binding* \newline $\beta \approx 1\text{--}5\text{ Mbps}$ (cyclic packets over deterministic command bus) | **BINDING** \newline $I^2 R$ copper winding dissipation, MOSFET switching losses                    | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t < 10\,\mu\text{s}$ (hard real-time PWM phase alignment & FOC)       | **BINDING** \newline Galvanic isolation, out-of-band analog E-stops, STO circuits               |

: **Handoffs-by-limits synthesis grid**: A five-by-five matrix mapping five canonical signal handoffs ($\mathcal{H}_1\text{--}\mathcal{H}_5$) across the Boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), Brain (@sec-brain), Body (@sec-body), and Nervous System (@sec-nervous) against five physical limits ($\tau, \beta, \mathcal{E}, \sigma_t, \mathcal{F}$). Cells marked *BINDING* are the budgets that drive selection; *Non-binding* means the scenario budget meets that dimension with margin. The matrix is the diagnostic rubric for Part I, in which safety and determinism appear as properties of isolated hardware boundaries, not software conventions. {#tbl-04-synthesis-grid tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

To ensure these budgets survive the lifecycle of the machine, every boundary condition in the grid is recorded as part of the machine's Transport Budget handoff record, the verifiable contract between hardware designers, systems engineers, and model developers. Each entry carries the six elements of a limit record (@sec-body-measuring-limits) and adds the fields that locate the limit at a handoff and say what kind of bound it is (@tbl-04-schema-notebook).

| Field Name               | Physical SI Units                                                | Structural Invariant & Description                                                                                                            |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `signal_id`              | dimensionless                                                    | Unique alphanumeric identifier (e.g. `SIG_VIO_01`, `SIG_TRQ_AX1`).                                                                            |
| `source_subsystem`       | dimensionless                                                    | Originating hardware or software module (`Camera_SerDes`, `Planner_VLA`).                                                                     |
| `destination_subsystem`  | dimensionless                                                    | Receiving hardware or software module (`State_Estimator`, `Safety_MCU`).                                                                      |
| `handoff`                | dimensionless                                                    | The handoff the signal crosses ($\mathcal{H}_1$ to $\mathcal{H}_5$).                                                                          |
| `physical_dimension`     | dimensionless                                                    | Target limit category ($\tau$, $\beta$, $\mathcal{E}$, $\sigma_t$, $\mathcal{F}$).                                                            |
| `value`                  | SI units ($\text{ms}$, $\text{MB/s}$, $\text{W}$, $\mu\text{s}$) | Allocated budget, or the measured distribution it is checked against; for $\mathcal{H}_4$, the chunk lease derived from the stopping budget.  |
| `conditions`             | as recorded                                                      | Payload, temperature, supply voltage, firmware build, and concurrent workload under which the value holds; the value lapses when they change. |
| `uncertainty`            | same as `value`                                                  | Error bound of the instrument or model that produced the value.                                                                               |
| `margin`                 | same as `value`                                                  | Engineering margin between the operating target and the breakdown threshold.                                                                  |
| `detector`               | dimensionless                                                    | Runtime monitor that catches an excursion (for example, a lease timer, a rail-voltage monitor, or a phase-current sensor).                    |
| `provenance`             | dimensionless                                                    | Source of the value, including its evidence category (measured, derived, datasheet, or illustrative).                                         |
| `bound_kind`             | dimensionless                                                    | `requirement`, `proven bound`, or `measured distribution`; only a proven bound may stand in for a worst case.                                 |
| `clock_domain`           | dimensionless                                                    | Clock on which every time-valued field is expressed; a handoff that feeds the permission path uses the safety microcontroller's clock.        |
| `verification_timestamp` | UTC timestamp                                                    | Date of bench falsification and sign-off; a log field, never an input to an age test.                                                         |

: **Conceptual fields of the handoff record**: The six limit-record elements of @sec-body-measuring-limits, extended with the handoff, bound kind, and clock domain that locate a limit in the machine and state what evidence supports it. {#tbl-04-schema-notebook tbl-colwidths="[22,24,54]"}

### Coupled budget synthesis for machine anatomy {#sec-nervous-coupled-budget}

The individual physical limits established across Part I do not operate in isolation: stopping distance, cognitive inference latency, memory bandwidth streaming, and deterministic command bus schedules converge into a single coupled timing equation. By linking the distance budget of the Body with the compute throughput of the Brain, the Nervous System establishes the allowable operational envelope for the entire embodied machine.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-coupled-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PART I COUPLED BUDGET: DISTANCE -> LEASE -> SUPPLY -> LEASE RULE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-coupled-budget.
# │ Goal:    Join Ch2's distance terms, this chapter's lease, and Ch3's supply
# │          rates into the lease rule for the running machine.
# │ Show:    ceiling 258.3 ms; running total 835.5 mm; intent sweep 98.0 ms,
# │          intent 5 Hz / 160 ms; chunk sweep 0.70 ms, 20 Hz / 40 ms;
# │          50 + 5 = 55 ms < 60 ms lease; upper limit 236.3 ms less age.
# │ How:     ceiling and running total read from MachineLeaseBudget;
# │          calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization on RM / AISLE; the 5 ms renewal jitter is a scenario assumption.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PartOneCoupledBudget:
    """The chunk lease as the meeting point of Part I's distance, timing, and supply budgets."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: illustrative
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (P99, incl. vision)
    t_renewal_jitter = MachineLeaseBudget.t_renewal_jitter  # category: chosen (from calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ceiling = MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling  # from calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget
    running_total = MachineLeaseBudget.running_total  # one source for the stopping budget

    intent_sweep = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=memory_from_params(RM.intent_model.parameters, BYTES_FP16 / param),
        memory_bandwidth=RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth,
        chunk_horizon=RM.chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=RM.dram_efficiency,
    )["t_stream"].to(millisecond)
    chunk_sweep = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=memory_from_params(RM.chunk_model.parameters, BYTES_FP16 / param),
        memory_bandwidth=RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth,
        chunk_horizon=RM.chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=RM.dram_efficiency,
    )["t_stream"].to(millisecond)

    t_chunk_period = (1 / f_chunk).to(millisecond)
    t_renewal_need = (t_chunk_period + t_renewal_jitter).to(millisecond)  # lease lower limit
    t_lease_upper = (t_ceiling - t_tick - t_bus - t_act).to(millisecond)  # before observation age
    mm_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_ceiling.magnitude - 258.333) < 5e-3, f"Pre-brake ceiling drifted: {t_ceiling}")
    check(abs(running_total.magnitude - 835.5) < 1e-6, f"Running total drifted: {running_total}")
    check(abs(intent_sweep.magnitude - 98.04) < 5e-3, f"Intent weight sweep drifted: {intent_sweep}")
    check(abs(chunk_sweep.magnitude - 0.700) < 5e-4, f"Chunk weight sweep drifted: {chunk_sweep}")
    check(abs(f_chunk.to(hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk rate drifted: {f_chunk}")
    check(abs(f_intent.to(hertz).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent rate drifted: {f_intent}")
    check(abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk inference latency drifted: {t_chunk}")
    check(abs(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude - 160.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent inference latency drifted: {t_intent}")
    check(abs(t_chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-6, f"Chunk period drifted: {t_chunk_period}")
    check(intent_sweep > t_lease and t_intent > t_lease, "The intent model must be unable to renew a chunk lease")
    check(t_chunk < t_chunk_period, "Chunk inference must finish within the chunk period")
    check(abs(t_renewal_need.magnitude - 55.0) < 1e-6, f"Lease lower limit drifted: {t_renewal_need}")
    check(t_renewal_need < t_lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus jitter must be shorter than the lease")
    check(abs(t_lease_upper.magnitude - 236.333) < 5e-3, f"Lease upper limit (before age) drifted: {t_lease_upper}")
    check(t_lease <= t_lease_upper - AISLE.perception_age, "Lease rule: lease must fit the ceiling after tick, bus, onset, and age")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    running_total_str = fmt_length(running_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    intent_sweep_str = fmt_latency(intent_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_intent_str = fmt_latency(t_intent, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(f_intent, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    chunk_sweep_str = fmt_latency(chunk_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    f_chunk_str = fmt_frequency(f_chunk, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_need_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_need, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_upper_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_upper, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mm_per_ms_str = fmt_length(mm_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

The three chapters of Part I each set terms of one budget, and the chunk lease is where they meet. @Sec-body-kinetic-momentum fixed the distance side. At its `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.v_str` drive limit the loaded machine must stop inside the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance at a rack end, and the braking term and the fixed overheads leave `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_ceiling_str` for everything that happens before braking force begins. @Sec-nervous-cadences spent part of that time. A proposer that stalls keeps its authority for one lease, the stop reaches the drives one tick and one bus cycle later, and the stopping budget stands at `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.running_total_str`.

The lease cannot be made as short as the budget would like, because a proposer must renew it. @Sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline established what each learned proposer can supply. The intent model's weights take `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.intent_sweep_str` to stream from memory once, before any vision work, and a full inference takes `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_intent_str`, so at `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.f_intent_str` it cannot renew a proposal every few tens of milliseconds. The chunk policy's weights stream in `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.chunk_sweep_str`, and at `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.f_chunk_str` it publishes a fresh chunk every `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_chunk_period_str`, each within its `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_chunk_str` P99 inference time, so it can.

These facts fix the **lease rule**\index{Chunk lease!lease rule} for this machine. The lease must outlast one chunk period plus an allowance for renewal jitter, which together set the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_renewal_need_str` floor of \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}. It must also fit inside the pre-brake ceiling once the tick, the bus cycle, and brake onset are reserved, which leaves `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_upper_str` less the observation age that @sec-perception measures. The chosen `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_str` sits just above the lower limit, because every millisecond of lease costs `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.mm_per_ms_str` at the drive limit, and later chapters add terms that need that distance.

Each chunk carries the base's velocity and the arm's joint targets together, so one lease governs both bodies, and when it lapses each body enters its own stop. The lease is sized on the base's `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_ceiling_str` pre-brake ceiling because that ceiling is tighter than the limit the arm's commitment sets. The same lease bounds the arm, and @sec-planning-handoff derives the arm's limit and checks its lease path and ceiling against its own clearance. The arm's evidence horizon bounds a different lease, the intent lease, which limits how long an admitted goal from the intent model stays valid, and the intent model's slower targets expire under it (@sec-intent-lease).

The $\mathcal{H}_4$ row of @tbl-04-synthesis-grid is this chapter's Transport Budget handoff record filled in, the third contract in the machine lineage following the Limit Record (@sec-body) and the Proposal Record (@sec-brain). Its value is the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_str` chunk lease handed from the chunk policy to the permission path, a `requirement` chosen inside limits derived from the stopping budget and valid up to the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.v_str` drive limit, loaded, on a dry floor, at the chunk period above; its margin is the span between the renewal floor and the ceiling-derived upper limit less the observation age, and its detector is the lease timer on the safety microcontroller, counted on that processor's own clock.

::: {#chk-nervous-handoffs-grid .callout-checkpoint title="The handoffs matrix and physical budgets"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-humanoid-fall-deadline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HUMANOID FALL TIMESCALE FOR THE PART I CAPSTONE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-coupled-budget, the Part I humanoid capstone
# │          (canon §3.7).
# │ Goal:    State the deadline a fall sets, in place of the stop's pre-brake
# │          ceiling, so the lease question can be asked of a biped.
# │ Show:    tau_fall = sqrt(z_c / g) ~ 303 ms for a 0.9 m center-of-mass height.
# │ How:     calc_inverted_pendulum_fall_time; the registry's humanoids carry no
# │          center-of-mass height, so z_c is a scenario input.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

class HumanoidFallDeadline:
    """Characteristic fall timescale of an upright biped modeled as an inverted pendulum."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    z_c = 0.9 * meter  # category: illustrative (scenario center-of-mass height; no registry field)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_fall = calc_inverted_pendulum_fall_time(effective_length=z_c).to(millisecond)
    t_fall_rounded = round(t_fall.magnitude) * millisecond  # prose says "about"

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_fall.magnitude - 302.9) < 0.5, f"Humanoid fall timescale drifted: {t_fall}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_fall_str = fmt_latency(t_fall_rounded, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

::: {#capstone-nervous-humanoid-crucible .callout-perspective title="A deadline set by a fall"}
**Question**: Does the split among proposer, lease, and permission path still hold when the deadline comes from a fall rather than a stop?

An upright biped diverges from balance on the characteristic timescale $\tau_{\text{fall}} = \sqrt{z_c/g}$, where $z_c$ is its center-of-mass height. Modeling the biped in the sagittal plane as an inverted pendulum of point mass $m$ pivoting above a contact point at height $z_c$, Newton's second law for a small angular deflection $\theta$ from vertical yields:
$$m z_c^2 \ddot{\theta} = m g z_c \sin\theta \implies \ddot{\theta} \approx \frac{g}{z_c} \theta$$
The characteristic equation $\ddot{\theta} - \omega_0^2 \theta = 0$ yields natural divergence modes $e^{\pm \omega_0 t}$ with natural frequency $\omega_0 = \sqrt{g/z_c}$. The unstable positive pole governs how quickly an unrecovered perturbation tilts out of control, with characteristic divergence timescale:
$$\tau_{\text{fall}} = \frac{1}{\omega_0} = \sqrt{\frac{z_c}{g}}$$
For an adult-scale humanoid with center of mass near hip height ($z_c = 0.9\,\text{m}$) and gravitational acceleration $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$, this evaluates to $\tau_{\text{fall}} = \sqrt{0.9 / 9.81} \approx 0.303\,\text{s} = 303\,\text{ms}$ (about `{python} HumanoidFallDeadline.t_fall_str`). This divergence timescale defines an unyielding physical deadline: if a foot placement or recovery step is not executed within $\tau_{\text{fall}}$, gravity accelerates the center of mass beyond the support polygon into an unrecoverable ground collision.

The split holds, and what changes is the deadline its terms answer to:

* **The lease is sized from the dynamic capture-point deadline.** On a wheeled mobile base, an expired lease commands mechanical deceleration to rest ($v \cdot T_{\text{lease}}$). On an underactuated biped, static halting is catastrophic: applying mechanical holding brakes mid-gait causes the torso to pivot forward into an uncontrolled ground collision. The lease fallback action therefore transitions from mechanical braking to **emergency capture-point step execution**. The lease, the tick, the bus cycle, and the observation age must strictly fit inside the time before the foot must touch down at the capture point ($\tau_{\text{fall}} \approx 303\text{ ms}$) to arrest sagittal angular momentum.
* **The intent model is still disqualified.** Its renewal period alone spends most of the fall timescale and leaves no room for the tick, the bus cycle, and the step itself, so only the chunk policy can renew a lease on this deadline.
* **Heat and supply sag limit the step.** The recovery step draws peak current in both legs at once, heating windings and sagging the supply (@sec-body-power-integrity), so the permission path must admit only a step that the supply and the windings can deliver at that moment.
:::

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-nervous-fallacies-pitfalls}

A block diagram draws a logical line between high-level deliberation and low-level enforcement, but physical hardware often connects them invisibly through shared power rails, interrupt lines, or back-channel diagnostic interfaces. These physical couplings dictate whether the permission loop remains standing when a complex subsystem fails.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Servicing a safety watchdog inside a high-priority timer interrupt rather than an application-verified safety loop.*

The mobile manipulator's self-watchdog removes drive power through the Safe Torque Off path of @sec-nervous-actuation-authority if it receives no feed within `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_self_watchdog_str`, because an enforcer that has stopped completing its checks can no longer command a controlled stop. Suppose engineers refresh it from a high-priority timer interrupt and the lower-priority enforcement task deadlocks. The interrupt continues firing every `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` tick even though the task has frozen and stopped checking torque limits, clearance, and chunk leases. The watchdog therefore stays fed while the enforcer has silently lost its safety function.

In distributed systems engineering, this represents the classic **liveness versus semantic correctness fallacy**: a node that responds to network ping heartbeats can be completely livelocked, thrashing on memory allocation, or deadlocked on an internal mutex. A watchdog service pulse must never assert mere scheduler activity; it must be conditioned on the successful, sequential retirement of all required verification stages (a windowed hardware watchdog pet conditioned on a monotonic task-completion token). An independent timer tick establishes only that hardware interrupt vectors still cycle, not that the controller has safely evaluated the machine's physical state (@sec-nervous-hardware-isolation).

**Architect's countermeasure**: Bind watchdog refresh pulses strictly to the verified completion of the safety loop's invariant checks, deploying windowed hardware watchdogs that trip on both execution underruns and spurious early feeds.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Leaving auxiliary diagnostic or calibration interfaces unmediated in production operation.*

Suppose the mobile manipulator validates base velocity proposals through its permission path, yet its drive-wheel motor drives retain an unmonitored serial calibration interface. A diagnostic daemon uses that interface to write a $35.0\text{ A}$ test value directly into an inverter register. The proposal mailbox still contains zero velocity, so checking that mailbox does not reveal the bypassed command. The drive wheels can then produce torque that no motion check ever saw or approved. True actuation authority includes every physical wire or digital interface capable of changing a power-stage register. Service interfaces therefore need operational interlocks or equivalent enforcement that prevents calibration writes from bypassing the controller during normal operation.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Electrically isolate, physically jumper, or cryptographically interlock all auxiliary diagnostic and calibration ports during operational modes, routing all register writes exclusively through the real-time enforcer.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Evaluating safety barrier invariants on commanded trajectory setpoints is equivalent to evaluating physical plant state.*

Suppose the machine's arm evaluates a control barrier function [@ames2019control] using commanded joint positions instead of load-side encoder measurements to reduce bus traffic. When a gear fails and the link moves away from its commanded trajectory, the interpolator continues producing valid setpoints. The enforcer still calculates that all is safe ($h(\mathbf{q}_{\text{cmd}}) > 0$), even as the physical link enters a forbidden region. Computing the wrong input faster cannot correct it. Safety enforcement belongs at the causal boundary (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary), so it must evaluate physical state measurements through a dependable sensory channel and account for their limitations; inspecting the command stream merely establishes what the planner intended, not where the heavy machinery actually is.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Close safety barrier evaluations strictly around verified, independent sensor measurements (optical load encoders, current shunts) rather than planned trajectory setpoints.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Nominal, fault-free operating logs are sufficient to prove physical architectural isolation.*

The mobile manipulator completes normal trials without a missed enforcement deadline. Those logs show behavior under a fault-free workload; they do not expose the hidden physical couplings that emerge only under faults. Qualification therefore injects power transients, floods communication buses, corrupts policy memory, and locks a shaft on a dynamometer. Each experiment must check an explicit response bound, such as whether locked-rotor detection clamps current within $2.0\text{ ms}$, rather than treating the absence of a crash as success. Evidence for isolation comes from exercising the claimed fault boundaries and measuring continued enforcement or the required safe transition.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Validate fault-domain independence through active fault-injection regimes (power sags, clock glitches, bus flooding, and memory corruption) with quantitative pass-fail response bounds.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Assuming zero packet loss in robotics middleware equates to deterministic real-time delivery.*

A common architectural error is deploying general-purpose publish-subscribe middleware (such as ROS 2 over DDS) configured with "Reliable" Quality of Service (QoS) on a cycle-critical control link. While Reliable QoS guarantees eventual packet delivery without data loss, it achieves this by buffering unacknowledged packets and retransmitting dropped frames across the network. When temporary bus congestion or wireless interference causes packet loss, the middleware triggers a retransmission storm. Transport latency surges from sub-millisecond nominal values to tens or hundreds of milliseconds, starving the motor drive of fresh setpoints. In physical motion control, lossless queuing is a hazard. Cycle-critical control requires either deterministic hardware buses (EtherCAT) or middleware configured for "Best Effort" delivery with a queue depth of one (lossy freshest-value delivery), where late packets are dropped immediately in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time rather than retransmitted.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Restrict general-purpose publish-subscribe middleware to supervisory perception and diagnostic streams. Use hardware time-triggered buses or zero-allocation, wait-free shared-memory mailboxes with depth-one freshest-value semantics for all cycle-critical actuation paths.
:::

## Summary {#sec-nervous-summary}

@Sec-body measured how far the loaded machine travels before it can stop, and @sec-brain measured what each learned proposer can supply and how quickly its evidence ages. This chapter set the permission path's check rate from the joint loop's stability latency margin, and it converted those two measurements into the time for which a proposal may drive the actuators. The result on the mobile manipulator is a chunk lease long enough to outlast one renewal of the chunk policy and short enough to fit inside the pre-brake ceiling, and the Transport Budget handoff record carries that lease, with its conditions and its evidence, to every later chapter. The lease and every other mechanism of this chapter remain claims until they have been exercised under compute delays, bus faults, bad proposals, sensor errors, and loss of braking authority. Part I opened on the irreversibility law (principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility}), and the lease closes Part I as a rule about authority, since motion that cannot be recalled may be commanded only for as long as the stopping budget can pay for its travel.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="The permission path and determinism"}
* **Proposal is not permission:** High-level learned models act strictly as unprivileged proposal engines ($p_t$). Physical write privilege over motor drive registers is reserved exclusively for the deterministic real-time enforcer, on silicon whose isolation from the proposer has been demonstrated.
* **Cadence is dictated by physics, not software:** The 4-tier concurrency hierarchy ($20\text{ kHz}$ FOC current regulation, $1\text{ kHz}$ kinematic enforcer checks, $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ action-chunk inference, and $1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$ multimodal deliberation) is governed by physical time constants ($\tau_e = L/R$), discrete phase-lag margins ($\Delta\phi = -\omega T_s / 2$), exposure horizons, and model execution budgets.
* **The exchange never waits, and every proposal expires:** The permission path reads the mailbox in one bounded attempt per tick and keeps its last validated chunk on a collision, and the proposal header's evidence time and expiry end that chunk's authority whether or not any cancellation arrives.
* **Worst-case bounds outrank empirical distributions:** A statistical latency percentile ($P_{99}$) cannot prove real-time safety. Deterministic certification requires analytical Response Time Analysis ($R_i = C_i + B_i + I_i \le D_i$), eliminating unbounded bus contention and memory allocations from the safety path.
* **The veto is only as independent as what it shares:** A permission path that shares a clock, a power rail, a memory bus, or silicon with the proposer can be silenced by the proposer's faults, so independence is a claim that fault injection must demonstrate, not a property of separate processes.
* **Stopping dynamics dimension the chunk lease:** On the mobile manipulator at its drive limit, the pre-brake ceiling is `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_str`. The chosen `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` lease sits just above the shortest lease the chunk policy can renew, and the path from its last renewal to brake onset spends `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_renewal_to_onset_str`, bringing the stopping budget to `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.running_total_str` of the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance.
* **A failure is an over-budget limit at one handoff:** The Transport Budget handoff record places each limit at one of five handoffs with its conditions, evidence category, and bound kind, so a regression is diagnosed against its allocated budget with like-for-like evidence.
:::

The Nervous System completes the three-part anatomy of the embodied machine by transforming the foundational law—*Proposal is not permission*—from an abstract design aspiration into an unyielding silicon reality. By placing cycle-deterministic permission gates, time-triggered buses, and bounded execution leases between statistical neural models and motor drive electronics, systems engineers insulate the physical world from computational tail latency and algorithmic hallucination. If a high-level cognitive model experiences an unhandled exception or an operating system thread hangs, the physical machine does not plunge forward in blind kinetic travel; the Nervous System detects the expired lease and instantly deploys a certified, dynamically feasible stopping suffix. With the anatomical container now fully specified—the Body setting physical limits, the Brain proposing candidate behaviors, and the Nervous System arbitrating real-time safety—the engineering challenge transitions from hardware architecture to behavioral acquisition.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From anatomy to closed-loop learning"}
With the Body (@sec-body), the Brain (@sec-brain), and the Nervous System of this chapter now specified, **Part I (The Machine Anatomy)** has assembled the physical container through three foundational contracts: the **Limit Record** bounding moving mass, the **Proposal Record** bounding cognitive deliberation, and the **Transport Budget** bounding the deterministic permission path that guards the causal boundary. Yet assembling this certified anatomy does not confer operational competence. A machine fresh off the assembly line cannot autonomously open a spring-latched cage door, clear a jammed warehouse conveyor, or recover when its gripper slips. Every teleoperated demonstration or imitation dataset gathered to teach it must cross the very transport boundary and permission enforcer built in this chapter—meaning human commands may be clamped, rate-limited, or overridden to protect physical hardware. In **Part II (Teaching the Machine)**, @sec-data therefore starts from the gap between the action requested and the motion the body delivered, establishing what an embodied demonstration dataset must record so that a neural policy learns the true physical task rather than the masking quirks of the enforcer that guarded it.
:::
